config.title: Compound Component (Tabs)

intro.title: Compound Component (Tabs)
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a Tabs component using React and TypeScript. You will learn the compound component pattern, which allows you to create flexible and reusable UI components by composing them together. The main technologies involved are React's Context API for state management and TypeScript interfaces for type safety. By the end, you will have a functional Tabs component where users can click between different tab panels to display content.
intro.usecase: Compound components like Tabs appear in nearly every modern web application where content needs to be organized in limited space. You'll find them in dashboard interfaces (like analytics platforms) where users switch between different data views, in e-commerce product pages that toggle between descriptions, reviews, and specifications, and in settings panels that organize configuration options into logical sections. As a developer, you'll implement this pattern when building navigation systems, content organizers, or any UI where users need to alternate between related content sections without overwhelming the interface.

objectives: Construct a Tabs compound component using React's children API and TypeScript interfaces
Implement a TabList component that renders clickable tab headers with proper TypeScript props
Configure a TabPanel component that displays content corresponding to the active tab
Initialize and manage the active tab state using React's useState hook with TypeScript typing
Bind click handlers to TabList items to update the active tab state
Control the conditional rendering of TabPanel content based on the active tab state
Integrate the Tabs, TabList, and TabPanel components into a working tab interface

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and the useState hook.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing modules for a project
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The imports are added at the top of the file.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to import both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the import statement. It should import React and useState from 'react'.

steps.title: Create the main Tabs component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named Tabs that accepts a children prop. Use a TypeScript interface to define the props.
steps.hint: Define an interface for the props, then create either a function Tabs(props: TabsProps) or const Tabs = (props: TabsProps) => {}. Return null for now.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the Tabs component here
steps.expectedOutcome: The Tabs component is defined with proper TypeScript props interface and returns null.
successCriteria: Tabs component exists with a children prop defined via a TypeScript interface.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the Tabs component with typed props.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you defined a TypeScript interface for the props and used it in the component.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Tabs component is missing or doesn't have the correct TypeScript props definition.

steps.title: Create the TabList component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named TabList that accepts a children prop. Define a TypeScript interface for its props and return the children wrapped in a <div> element.
steps.hint: Define an interface for the props, then create the component that returns children inside a div.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a TabList component that can wrap child elements.
successCriteria: TabList component is defined with a TypeScript interface and returns children inside a div.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure TabList has a children prop with a TypeScript interface and returns the children inside a div.
steps.feedbackWrong: The TabList component isn't defined correctly. Check that it accepts children and returns them in a div.

steps.title: Create the Tab component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named Tab that accepts props for id, isActive, and onClick using a TypeScript interface.
steps.hint: Define an interface for the props first, then create the component that returns a button element.
steps.expectedOutcome: A Tab component is defined with typed props and returns a button element.
successCriteria: Uses a TypeScript interface for props
Props include id, isActive, and onClick
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your Tab component accepts all three props (id, isActive, onClick) using a TypeScript interface and returns a button.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Tab component isn't defined correctly. Check that you've created a functional component with the correct props interface.

steps.title: Create the TabPanels component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named TabPanels that accepts a children prop using a TypeScript interface.
steps.hint: Define an interface for the props, then create a component that returns its children.
steps.expectedOutcome: A TabPanels component is defined with proper TypeScript typing for its children prop.
successCriteria: TabPanels component exists with an interface defining children as React.ReactNode and returns children.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure to define an interface for the props and have the component return its children.
steps.feedbackWrong: The TabPanels component isn't properly defined yet. Create a functional component named TabPanels with a children prop using TypeScript.

steps.title: Initialize active tab state in Tabs
steps.instruction: Inside the Tabs component, use the useState hook to declare a state variable called 'activeTab' with an initial value of 0. Provide an explicit TypeScript type annotation: <number>.
steps.hint: Remember to call useState with the initial value and destructure the returned array into the state variable and setter function.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: state with type annotation
const [count, setCount] = useState<number>(0);
steps.expectedOutcome: The Tabs component will have a state variable 'activeTab' initialized to 0, ready to track which tab is currently active.
successCriteria: The useState hook is called inside the Tabs component
A state variable named 'activeTab' is declared
The initial value is set to 0
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using useState with the correct syntax, including the type annotation <number>.
steps.feedbackWrong: The state wasn't properly initialized. Check that you're calling useState<number>(0) inside the Tabs component.

steps.title: Define tab change handler in Tabs
steps.instruction: Inside the Tabs component, define a function named handleTabChange that takes an index parameter and updates the active tab state using the setActiveTab function.
steps.hint: The function should accept a number parameter (the tab index) and call setActiveTab with that value.
steps.expectedOutcome: The Tabs component now has a handleTabChange function that can update the active tab state when called with a tab index.
successCriteria: A handleTabChange function is defined inside Tabs that accepts an index parameter and calls setActiveTab with it.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your handleTabChange function accepts an index parameter and calls setActiveTab with that index to update the state.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleTabChange function should be defined inside the Tabs component and update the activeTab state when called.

steps.title: Pass state and handler via context in Tabs
steps.instruction: Create a React context and a provider inside the Tabs component to share activeTab and handleTabChange with child components.
steps.hint: Use React.createContext to create a context, then wrap the component's children with a context provider that passes the values.
steps.expectedOutcome: A context is created and a provider is set up inside Tabs, ready to pass activeTab and handleTabChange to child components.
successCriteria: React.createContext is used to create a context, and a provider is returned from Tabs that wraps children and passes activeTab and handleTabChange as values.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started setting up the context, but make sure to create the context with React.createContext and wrap the children with a provider that passes both activeTab and handleTabChange.
steps.feedbackWrong: The context and provider aren't set up correctly. Use React.createContext to create a context, then return a provider from Tabs that passes activeTab and handleTabChange as values.

steps.title: Consume context in Tab and TabPanel components
steps.instruction: Inside the Tab component, use the useContext hook to access the activeTab and handleTabChange values from the TabsContext.
steps.hint: Call useContext with TabsContext as the argument and destructure the returned object to get activeTab and handleTabChange.
steps.expectedOutcome: The Tab component will have access to the activeTab state and handleTabChange function from the TabsContext.
successCriteria: Tab component uses useContext with TabsContext
activeTab and handleTabChange are destructured from the context
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using useContext with TabsContext and destructuring both activeTab and handleTabChange.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Tab component should use useContext to access the TabsContext values. Try using: const { activeTab, handleTabChange } = useContext(TabsContext);

steps.title: Assemble the compound component structure
steps.instruction: In the Tabs component, return the compound structure: a TabList containing Tab children, followed by a TabPanels containing TabPanel children, all wrapped in the context provider.
steps.hint: Place TabList and TabPanels as direct children of the context provider. Inside TabList, add Tab components with index props. Inside TabPanels, add TabPanel components with matching index props.
steps.expectedOutcome: The Tabs component returns the full compound structure with TabList, Tab, TabPanels, and TabPanel components properly nested and wired through context.
successCriteria: Tabs returns a JSX structure containing TabList and TabPanels as children of the context provider, with Tab and TabPanel components inside them using index props.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're returning the full structure: TabList with Tab children, TabPanels with TabPanel children, all wrapped in the context provider.
steps.feedbackWrong: The structure isn't complete yet. Remember to return TabList and TabPanels as children of the context provider, with Tab and TabPanel components inside them using index props.
